newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council registers end of Albania peacekeeping.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council registers end of Albania peacekeeping.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Thursday registered the end of a peacekeeping mission it authorized for Albania, with Italy saying the world should have moved as quickly in Bosnia and Rwanda.

In a statement read at a formal meeting after hours of scripted speeches, the council said the mandate of the 7,000-strong Italian-led force had been fulfilled successfully but that the Albanian people and leaders had primary responsiblity for the future of their country.
Albania was swept by violence in January when a string of popular "get-rich-quick" schemes collapsed and tens of thousands of people lost their savings.

Italy's U.N. Ambassador Paulo Fulci said that if the international community had acted with the same speed and determination in Bosnia and in Central Africa "thousands of lives would probably have been spared and immense suffering and destruction prevented."

A 10-nation force of 7,000, led by Italy and authorized but not organized by the United Nations, was sent to Albania in April after near-anarchy swept the impoverished nation. The last of the soldiers left earlier this week after restoring some order and protecting aid groups and relief supplies.

Fulci, responsible for getting Security Council endorsement for the force on March 28, said the action had helped reverse Albania's decline with the country "back on the road toward normality and internal security."

The International Committee of the Red Cross sounded a note of caution, however. Its envoy, Sylvie Junod, told the council that Albania still suffered from the "absence of law and order" despite government promises to restore security.
"The government is far from being in control of the entire territory. Banditry of all types is rife, and insecurity prevails in most of the country," she said.

Fulci also used the occasion to say that the operation was a useful model for future peacekeeping activities. He said it was organized with speed by a group of countries despite the risks involved, and had received approval from the council within 12 hours of a request.
The force was planned rapidly among troop-contributing nations, had a date for its departure and was integrated and followed up by political and economic projects.

Fulci also said the force "refrained from any kind of police activities" in line with its requested U.N. mandate to be "neutral and impartial." Its main purpose was to facilitate and protect humanitarian assistance.
The multinational force had been criticized for not stopping the violence over the past month in which 1,500 people were killed.
